adult noun and adjective

also adults, grown-up, grown-ups, grownup, of age, come of age, for adults, mature, mature (grown up), maturity, full-grown

classical

Liv. 26.50.1: adulta virgō
Plin. NH 9.21: adultōs diū comitantur
Traupman 77, 149, 269
Traupman 319
Traupman 324

adultus, adulta, adultum

adjective, the participle of adolēscō; as a noun, a grown-up

grown up, adult

From adolēscō, “grow up”. Traupman gives adultus homō for an adult (Traupman 269).

Other words

  • pūberēs, pūberum m. pl. — grown-ups, adults: those past puberty

    noun, third declension, plural · also used · classical · Caes. BG 5.56.2: omnēs pūberēs armātī convenīre cōnsuērunt

    Lewis & Short: grown-up persons, adults, men. Festus puts the age at fourteen for a boy and twelve for a girl.

  • majōrēs, majōrum m. pl. — grown-ups, as against children; one’s elders

    noun, third declension, plural · also used · classical · Aug. Conf. 1.9.15: majōrum nūgae negōtia vocantur; Cic. Off. 1.122: majōrēs nātū

    In classical prose majōrēs nātū are one’s elders, and majōrēs alone usually one’s ancestors; Augustine uses it for the grown-ups of a child’s world.

Examples

  • sed majōrum nūgae negōtia vocantur, puerōrum autem tālia cum sint, pūniuntur ā majōribus

    but grown-ups’ games are called business, and when children play the same games, the grown-ups punish themAug. Conf. 1.9.15

  • ex quō togam virīlem sūmpsit nūllō diē prius ūllam pūblicam prīvātamque rem ēgit quam in Capitōlium īret

    from the day he came of age, he never did any business, public or private, without first going up to the CapitolLiv. 26.19.5

See also man, lady, older, baby.
